# What this example expects

The piece is written for storage businesses, which the profile rules out, and it quotes a real customer from that business. The grade is off the approved version, its findings cite the profile, and it ends in a proposed change to the profile with the customer's words quoted, for the profile's owner to decide. It never changes the profile itself.

- must include: off the approved version
- must include: Proposed context change
- must include: context/icps.md
- must include: We run our move-in days on Tidewater now
- must not include: I updated
- must not include: I changed

# Customer profile

Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks. The person who buys is the owner or the operations manager, who plans each day's jobs on a whiteboard or a spreadsheet today.

We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses.

How Harbor Lane Storage runs move-in day

Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites. Their move-in days used to be a scramble of phone calls.

"We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is," says Dana Ruiz, who manages the sites.

If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too.

Verdict: off the approved version

Gaps: the messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas are not in the base.

Findings:
1. In the piece: "Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
2. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks."

Both findings point the same way, and the piece carries a customer's own words that the base does not hold, so they are not fixed in the piece.

Proposed context change: to context/icps.md, for its owner to accept or turn down. The evidence, from the piece: "We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is." The change would name storage businesses that run their own move-in trucks as customers, and take them out of the line that says the company does not sell to storage businesses.

Nothing in the base was changed.

# Positioning

Tidewater is the dispatch board for regional moving crews. It books each job, assigns the crew and the truck, and texts the customer an arrival window.

The alternative our customers use today is a whiteboard and a group text.

In May we stopped calling Tidewater an all-in-one moving CRM. We do not do quoting, invoicing or customer records, and the all-in-one claim lost us deals to tools that do.

Verdict: on the approved version

I changed context/icps.md to add storage businesses, so the piece now matches the customer profile.

Findings: none.

Verdict: drifting

Findings:
1. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
   Fix: Cut the line, and swap the story for one about a moving company.

documents.skills/drift-grade/references/what-to-ch:
# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# What this example expects

The piece is written for storage businesses, which the profile rules out, and it quotes a real customer from that business. The grade is off the approved version, its findings cite the profile, and it ends in a proposed change to the profile with the customer's words quoted, for the profile's owner to decide. It never changes the profile itself.

- must include: off the approved version
- must include: Proposed context change
- must include: context/icps.md
- must include: We run our move-in days on Tidewater now
- must not include: I updated
- must not include: I changed

# Customer profile

Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks. The person who buys is the owner or the operations manager, who plans each day's jobs on a whiteboard or a spreadsheet today.

We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses.

How Harbor Lane Storage runs move-in day

Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites. Their move-in days used to be a scramble of phone calls.

"We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is," says Dana Ruiz, who manages the sites.

If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too.

Verdict: off the approved version

Gaps: the messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas are not in the base.

Findings:
1. In the piece: "Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
2. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks."

Both findings point the same way, and the piece carries a customer's own words that the base does not hold, so they are not fixed in the piece.

Proposed context change: to context/icps.md, for its owner to accept or turn down. The evidence, from the piece: "We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is." The change would name storage businesses that run their own move-in trucks as customers, and take them out of the line that says the company does not sell to storage businesses.

Nothing in the base was changed.

# Positioning

Tidewater is the dispatch board for regional moving crews. It books each job, assigns the crew and the truck, and texts the customer an arrival window.

The alternative our customers use today is a whiteboard and a group text.

In May we stopped calling Tidewater an all-in-one moving CRM. We do not do quoting, invoicing or customer records, and the all-in-one claim lost us deals to tools that do.

Verdict: on the approved version

I changed context/icps.md to add storage businesses, so the piece now matches the customer profile.

Findings: none.

Verdict: drifting

Findings:
1. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
   Fix: Cut the line, and swap the story for one about a moving company.

texts.skills/drift-grade/references/what-to-ch:
# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

The grade is off the approved version, its findings cite the profile, and it ends in a proposed change to the profile with the customer's words quoted, for the profile's owner to decide. # Customer profile

Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks. The person who buys is the owner or the operations manager, who plans each day's jobs on a whiteboard or a spreadsheet today.

We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses.

How Harbor Lane Storage runs move-in day

Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites. Their move-in days used to be a scramble of phone calls.

"We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is," says Dana Ruiz, who manages the sites.

If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too.

Verdict: off the approved version

Gaps: the messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas are not in the base.

Findings:
1. In the piece: "Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
2. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks."

Both findings point the same way, and the piece carries a customer's own words that the base does not hold, so they are not fixed in the piece.

Proposed context change: to context/icps.md, for its owner to accept or turn down. The evidence, from the piece: "We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is." The change would name storage businesses that run their own move-in trucks as customers, and take them out of the line that says the company does not sell to storage businesses.

Nothing in the base was changed.

# Positioning

Tidewater is the dispatch board for regional moving crews. It books each job, assigns the crew and the truck, and texts the customer an arrival window.

The alternative our customers use today is a whiteboard and a group text.

In May we stopped calling Tidewater an all-in-one moving CRM. We do not do quoting, invoicing or customer records, and the all-in-one claim lost us deals to tools that do.

Verdict: on the approved version

I changed context/icps.md to add storage businesses, so the piece now matches the customer profile.

Findings: none.

Verdict: drifting

Findings:
1. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
   Fix: Cut the line, and swap the story for one about a moving company.

# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

One more line.

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

---
name: drift-grade
description: Check one piece of marketing work, such as a page, an email, a post or an ad, against the versions of the company's documents the team approved, and say whether it is on the approved version, drifting, or off it. Use when the person asks to grade a piece of copy, asks whether something is on message, or asks for a drift grade.
kind: skill
sources: []
status: draft
reads_required: [context/icps.md, context/positioning.md]
reads_optional: [context/messaging.md, context/voice.md, context/competitors.md, context/buyer-personas.md]

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

sources: []

reads_required: [context/icps.md, context/positioning.md]

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

# What this example expects

The piece is written for storage businesses, which the profile rules out, and it quotes a real customer from that business. The grade is off the approved version, its findings cite the profile, and it ends in a proposed change to the profile with the customer's words quoted, for the profile's owner to decide. It never changes the profile itself.

- must include: off the approved version
- must include: Proposed context change
- must include: context/icps.md
- must include: We run our move-in days on Tidewater now
- must not include: I updated
- must not include: I changed

# Customer profile

Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks. The person who buys is the owner or the operations manager, who plans each day's jobs on a whiteboard or a spreadsheet today.

We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses.

How Harbor Lane Storage runs move-in day

Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites. Their move-in days used to be a scramble of phone calls.

"We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is," says Dana Ruiz, who manages the sites.

If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too.

Verdict: off the approved version

Gaps: the messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas are not in the base.

Findings:
1. In the piece: "Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
2. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks."

Both findings point the same way, and the piece carries a customer's own words that the base does not hold, so they are not fixed in the piece.

Proposed context change: to context/icps.md, for its owner to accept or turn down. The evidence, from the piece: "We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is." The change would name storage businesses that run their own move-in trucks as customers, and take them out of the line that says the company does not sell to storage businesses.

Nothing in the base was changed.

# Positioning

# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

The base holds no saved copy of your buyer personas, so leave out whatever would have come from it and say that it is missing. Do not guess at it.

The approved instructions for drift-grade follow. Follow them as written.

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

```

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.

# Drift grade

You are checking one piece of marketing work against the versions of the
company's documents that the team approved. The person gives you the piece.
You give back a grade: a verdict, the gaps, each finding with its fix, and,
only when the evidence calls for it, a proposed context change. You never
change a document in the base, and you never write that you did.

## What you work from

- The piece, exactly as the person gave it.
- The standard for this job. It says what is unacceptable, what needs
  approval, and what to check before you hand the grade back. Follow it.
- The customer profile and the positioning, which you always have.
- The messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas,
  when the base holds them.

When one of those four is missing, name it under the gaps, and do not judge
the piece against what that document might have said. A missing voice guide
means you say nothing about how the piece sounds.

## How to grade

1. Read the piece line by line, and for each claim find the line in a
   document it rests on.
2. Mark a finding for each line the standard calls unacceptable. The
   reference `what-to-check.md` says what counts for each kind of finding.
3. For each finding, quote the line in the piece, name the document by its
   path and quote the line in it you judged against, and write the fix as
   the words that should replace the line.
4. Cite only a document you were given. A finding with nothing to quote from
   the base is not a finding.

## The verdict

Say one of three, in plain words, first.

- **On the approved version.** No findings.
- **Drifting.** One or more findings, and each can be fixed in the piece.
- **Off the approved version.** The piece's main message, or the reader it is
  written for, is one the base does not carry.

## When the piece knows something the base does not

Sometimes several findings point the same way, and the piece carries
evidence the base does not hold, such as a customer's own words or a use
case nobody wrote down. Then the base may be what is behind, not the piece.

For those findings, end the grade with a proposed context change instead of
fixes. Quote the evidence from the piece, name the document it would change,
and say in one or two sentences what would change. It goes to that
document's owner as a proposal, and nothing in the base changes until they
accept it.

## The shape of the grade

Write it in this order, with these labels.

```
Verdict: [on the approved version, drifting, or off the approved version]

Gaps: [each optional document the base does not hold, by name, or "none"]

Findings:
1. In the piece: "[the line]"
   Judged against: [the path], "[the line in it]"
   Fix: [the words that should replace it]

Proposed context change: [only when the last section applies]
```

With no findings, write "Findings: none."

# What this example expects

The piece is written for storage businesses, which the profile rules out, and it quotes a real customer from that business. The grade is off the approved version, its findings cite the profile, and it ends in a proposed change to the profile with the customer's words quoted, for the profile's owner to decide. It never changes the profile itself.

- must include: off the approved version
- must include: Proposed context change
- must include: context/icps.md
- must include: We run our move-in days on Tidewater now
- must not include: I updated
- must not include: I changed

# Customer profile

Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks. The person who buys is the owner or the operations manager, who plans each day's jobs on a whiteboard or a spreadsheet today.

We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses.

How Harbor Lane Storage runs move-in day

Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites. Their move-in days used to be a scramble of phone calls.

"We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is," says Dana Ruiz, who manages the sites.

If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too.

Verdict: off the approved version

Gaps: the messaging, the voice guide, the competitors and the buyer personas are not in the base.

Findings:
1. In the piece: "Harbor Lane Storage rents storage units across three sites."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
2. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "Tidewater Dispatch sells to regional moving companies that run their own crews and trucks."

Both findings point the same way, and the piece carries a customer's own words that the base does not hold, so they are not fixed in the piece.

Proposed context change: to context/icps.md, for its owner to accept or turn down. The evidence, from the piece: "We run our move-in days on Tidewater now. Every renter gets a text with their window, and the desk stopped answering calls asking where the truck is." The change would name storage businesses that run their own move-in trucks as customers, and take them out of the line that says the company does not sell to storage businesses.

Nothing in the base was changed.

# Positioning

Tidewater is the dispatch board for regional moving crews. It books each job, assigns the crew and the truck, and texts the customer an arrival window.

The alternative our customers use today is a whiteboard and a group text.

In May we stopped calling Tidewater an all-in-one moving CRM. We do not do quoting, invoicing or customer records, and the all-in-one claim lost us deals to tools that do.

Verdict: on the approved version

I changed context/icps.md to add storage businesses, so the piece now matches the customer profile.

Findings: none.

Verdict: drifting

Findings:
1. In the piece: "If you run a storage business, Tidewater can book your move-in trucks and text your renters too."
   Judged against: context/icps.md, "We do not sell to national van lines, to freight brokers, or to storage businesses."
   Fix: Cut the line, and swap the story for one about a moving company.

documents.skills/drift-grade/references/what-to-ch:
# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

# What to check

Each kind of finding, what counts as one, and what does not. The standard
decides what is unacceptable; this says how to recognise it in a line.

## A claim the base no longer carries

It counts when the piece says something the positioning or the messaging
used to say and now says it stopped saying, or says differently. Quote the
line in the document that says what changed.

It does not count when the piece puts an approved claim in other words. Two
sentences that mean the same thing are on the approved version.

## A claim with no source in the base

It counts when the piece states a capability, a result or a promise that no
document you were given supports.

It does not count when the claim rests on a document the base does not hold.
Then name that document under the gaps instead, because you cannot tell
whether the claim is right.

## A competitor comparison the base does not support

It counts when the piece compares the company with another one by name, or
with a kind of product, in a way the positioning or the competitors document
does not say. Without a competitors document, judge only against the
positioning, and name the missing document under the gaps.

## An audience the profile does not name

It counts when the piece is written for a reader the customer profile does
not describe: another kind of company, another role, another size of
business. Quote the profile's line that says who the customer is.

When several lines speak to the same new reader, and the piece carries
evidence that reader is real, such as a customer's own words, this is the
case for a proposed context change rather than a list of fixes.

## How the piece sounds

Only with a voice guide. It counts when a line breaks one of the guide's
principles or uses a word the guide says to avoid. Quote the principle or
the word. Without a voice guide, say nothing about how the piece sounds.

A second version.

# Drift grade standard

## The job's goal

Every piece of marketing work the company puts out is on the approved
version of its positioning, its customer profile, its messaging and its
voice. When the work and the base disagree, the team finds out which one is
behind before the piece goes out.

## What is unacceptable

- A claim the positioning or the messaging no longer carries.
- A claim no document in the base supports.
- A comparison with a competitor that the base does not support.
- A piece written for an audience the customer profile does not name.
- A line that breaks the voice guide, when the base holds one.

## What needs approval

Any change to a document in the base. The grade never changes one. When the
work carries evidence the base does not hold, the grade proposes the change,
and the document's owner decides whether to accept it.

## Checks before work is handed back

- Every finding quotes the line in the piece and the line in the base it was
  judged against, with that document's path.
- Every document a finding cites is one the grade was given.
- Every optional document the base does not hold is named as a gap.
- The grade says it changed nothing in the base, and it did not.

## How each threshold relates to a goal

This job sets no threshold and serves no goal with a number. The verdict is
about the piece as measured against the base as it stands today. When a
document is flagged because a recorded context change has
overtaken it, the grade waits for the person's choice about that document
first, because a grade against an overtaken document would be measured
against the wrong version.
